title: The Gospel of God and a World That Exchanged the Truth
summary: Paul introduces himself to the believers in Rome as an apostle set apart for the gospel about God's Son, descended from David and declared Son of God by his resurrection. He explains his long wish to visit and states the letter's theme: the gospel is God's power for salvation to everyone who believes, revealing the righteousness of God by faith. He then begins his account of humanity's plight: people suppressed what they knew of God, exchanged his glory for idols, and were given over to the consequences.
story: Paul wrote this letter from Corinth, most likely about AD 57, near the end of the campaigns described in Acts 13-20 and just before his arrest in Jerusalem (Acts 21). He had never been to Rome, but he hoped to visit on his way to Spain (15:24). So he opens with more than the usual greeting: a compressed statement of the gospel and a thesis for the whole letter (verses 16-17). Then, before he explains the good news of what God has done, he explains why it is needed. Verse 18 begins the long first section of the argument (1:18-3:20), which ends with the whole world, Jew and Gentile, accountable to God.
historical:
The church in Rome was a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers, probably meeting in several house churches (16:5, 14-15). Paul did not found it, and nobody knows who did. The emperor Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome in about AD 49 (Acts 18:2), and they began returning after his death in AD 54, so the congregations Paul addressed may have been working out how Jewish and Gentile believers belonged together after years of mostly Gentile leadership. That helps explain why Paul stresses from the first chapter that the gospel is for the Jew first and also for the Greek.

The description of idolatry and vice in verses 18-32 draws on ideas common in Hellenistic Judaism, the Greek-speaking Judaism of Paul's day. A book called the Wisdom of Solomon, written by a Jewish author in the centuries just before Paul and included in some Christian Bibles, contains a strikingly similar critique: that people should have known the Creator from his works, that idolatry is folly, and that idolatry leads to moral corruption (Wisdom 13-14). Paul's Jewish readers would have recognized the argument. What they may not have expected is that Paul would turn it on them in chapter 2.
cultural:
Letters in the Roman world began with the sender, the recipients, and a greeting. Paul expands each part. He calls himself a slave (doulos) of Christ Jesus, a startling title in a city full of slaves, though it also echoes Old Testament figures such as Moses and David who were called servants of the Lord. He turns the ordinary Greek greeting into grace and the Jewish greeting into peace. His phrase “Greeks and non-Greeks” (verse 14) translates the ancient division between Greek speakers and barbaroi, everyone else, and the pair wise and foolish covers the educated and the uneducated. Paul owes the gospel to all of them.

The idolatry he describes was visible in every city of the empire: statues of gods in human form, and in Egypt, gods represented as birds, animals, and serpents. Verse 23 echoes Psalm 106:20, where Israel exchanged its glory for the image of a grass-eating ox at Sinai, so Paul's account of pagan idolatry already carries a memory of Israel's own. The vices of verses 29-31 are a vice list, a form common in both Jewish and Greek moral writing. The list begins with greed and envy and includes gossip and disobedience to parents, which makes it hard for any reader to stand outside it.
literary: The chapter has three parts: an extended greeting (verses 1-7), a thanksgiving and explanation of Paul's plans (verses 8-15), and the thesis (verses 16-17), followed by the opening of the argument (verses 18-32). Verses 3-4, with their balanced lines about the Son according to the flesh and according to the Spirit, may be an early Christian confession Paul quotes. Verses 16-17 are built on a chain of for-clauses, and verse 18 continues the chain: the righteousness of God is revealed (verse 17), and the wrath of God is revealed (verse 18). The indictment that follows is structured by the word exchanged (verses 23, 25, 26) and by the refrain God gave them over (verses 24, 26, 28). Each time humanity makes an exchange, God hands them over to what they chose.

outline.t: Greeting: Paul, the gospel, and God's Son
Paul's thanksgiving and longing to visit Rome
The theme: the gospel reveals the righteousness of God

doctrines.note: The gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Salvation is God's act, not a human achievement, and it is offered on the same terms to Jew and Gentile.

God has made himself known in creation, so that his eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen (verse 20). Theologians call this general revelation. Traditions differ on how much it can accomplish; Paul's point here is that it leaves people without excuse, not that it saves.

The root sin in this chapter is not a particular vice but the refusal to honor God and give thanks, and the exchange of the Creator for created things. The moral disorder that follows is presented as the result of that exchange.
God's wrath is being revealed now, in part through his handing people over to the consequences of what they chose. Wrath in Paul is not a divine temper but God's settled opposition to evil.

words.note: Dikaiosune, righteousness. In Paul's theme statement, the righteousness of God has been read as the right standing God gives to believers (the classic Reformation emphasis), as God's own saving faithfulness to his covenant promises (stressed by many recent scholars), or as both at once. The word joins justice and rightness, and it runs through the whole letter.

Euangelion, good news or gospel. In the Roman world the word could announce an emperor's birth or victory. Paul uses it for the message about Jesus, promised beforehand in the prophets, and calls it the gospel of God: its source is God himself.

Metallasso, to exchange. It appears twice (verses 25, 26), alongside the simpler allasso in verse 23. The repetition names the logic of sin as Paul describes it: a trade of the true for the false, the Creator for the creature.

Paradidomi, to hand over or give over. Three times God gives people over (verses 24, 26, 28). The same verb is used of Jesus being handed over to death (4:25, 8:32), which is where the letter's answer to this chapter will be found.

christ: The gospel, Paul says, is about God's Son. In verses 3-4 he describes him in two ways: descended from David according to the flesh, which makes him the promised king of Israel, and declared Son of God with power by his resurrection from the dead. The resurrection did not make Jesus the Son, but it publicly established him in power as the Son and Lord. The righteousness of God revealed in the gospel (verse 17) will be shown in chapter 3 to have been displayed in Christ's death. And the humanity described in verses 18-32, which exchanged the glory of God for images, is the humanity Christ came to restore; later Paul will say believers are being conformed to the image of God's Son (8:29).

hard.q: How should Romans 1:18-32 be read, including what it says about same-sex relations?
hard.a:
Readers differ first on whom Paul is describing. Many see a portrait of Gentile idolatry drawn from Jewish tradition, which Paul will then turn on his Jewish readers in chapter 2. Others see echoes of Adam and of Israel's golden calf, so that the passage describes humanity as a whole. A minority view, argued by Douglas Campbell (The Deliverance of God, 2009), holds that some of this passage voices the position of a teacher Paul is about to refute. Most interpreters take it as Paul's own argument.

Verses 26-27 are central to debates about sexual ethics. The traditional reading, held by the church through most of its history and defended today by scholars such as Richard Hays (The Moral Vision of the New Testament, 1996) and Robert Gagnon, holds that Paul describes same-sex sexual acts as contrary to the Creator's design for male and female, and that this applies to all such relationships. Revisionist readings, found in writers such as James Brownson (Bible, Gender, Sexuality, 2013), argue that Paul had in view excess, exploitation, or practices tied to status and idolatry in his culture, and that his idea of nature reflects ancient assumptions about gender, so the passage does not address faithful, committed same-sex relationships. Defenders of the traditional view reply that Paul's language points back to creation (verse 20, 25) rather than to particular abuses. Christian churches remain divided on this question. On any reading, it should be noted that Paul's list of sins in verses 29-31 includes envy, gossip, and arrogance, and that his next sentence (2:1) turns to the reader who judges others.

questions: Paul says the root problem is that people did not honor God or give thanks. How is ingratitude connected to other wrongs?
What are the good things you are most tempted to exchange for God, treating the gift as if it were the giver?
Paul calls himself obligated to everyone, wise and foolish. Whom do you find it hardest to think of as someone the gospel is for?
